mainTopic: How the wording of a קונם vow decides what is forbidden: replacements and growths of the vowed item, a wife's handiwork, and where the time limit עד הפסח is placed
overview: This amud is a משנה about how the exact wording of a קונם vow changes what it forbids. If a person puts the ban on the fruit itself ('קונם upon me'), then whatever he trades it for and whatever grows from it are forbidden too. If he only forbids his own eating ('that I eat'), the replacements and growths are permitted. The exception is a plant whose seed never breaks down, where even growths of growths stay forbidden. The same rules apply when a husband forbids his wife's handiwork to himself. The משנה then shows that where 'until פסח' sits in the sentence matters. Next to 'I will not eat,' it ends the ban at פסח. Next to 'what you make,' it marks which items are forbidden, and those stay forbidden after פסח. It ends with a ban on benefit until פסח that takes effect if she goes to her father's house before the festival.

steps.title: Making the fruit itself forbidden includes replacements and growths
steps.stepSummary: If someone says 'these fruits are קונם upon me' (or 'upon my mouth' or 'to my mouth'), he may not eat the fruits, anything traded for them, or anything that grows from them.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If someone says 'These fruits are קונם upon me,' or 'They are קונם upon my mouth,' or 'They are קונם to my mouth,' he is forbidden to eat their replacements and their growths.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה opens with the first type of vow wording, where the person puts the forbidden status on the fruit itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: All three phrasings make the fruit itself into a forbidden object, something like a sacred item. Because the fruit itself carries the ban, the ban moves on to what is traded for it and to what grows from it. This is the strict side of the contrast that comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A word used to make a vow; it makes something forbidden like a sacred offering
Upon me; the item is forbidden to me
Their replacements; things gotten in exchange for them
Their growths; what grows when they are planted

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
"These fruits are konam upon me,"
"They are konam upon my mouth,"
"They are konam to my mouth" —
he is forbidden in their replacements and in their growths.
phrases.notes: 'Replacements' means whatever he trades it for, and 'growths' means whatever grows from it.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow that puts the ban on the item itself also forbids its replacements and growths.

steps.title: Forbidding only the eating leaves replacements and growths permitted
steps.stepSummary: If he says 'קונם that I eat' or 'that I taste,' replacements and growths are permitted. This holds only for plants whose seed rots away. If the seed stays whole, even growths of growths are forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said '...that I eat' or '...that I taste,' he is permitted to have their replacements and their growths. This is with an item whose seed disappears. But with an item whose seed does not disappear, even growths of growths are forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the lenient contrast: when the vow only forbids his act of eating, the ban does not spread to replacements or growths. It then adds a limit to that leniency.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the ban is on his eating these specific fruits, not on the fruits as objects, so things traded for them or grown from them are new and permitted. But if the planted seed never breaks down, like a bulb that keeps regrowing, the original forbidden item is still there inside the new growth. So even growths of growths stay forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: That I eat; the vow forbids the act of eating
An item whose seed rots away once planted

steps.confusionAlert: The phrase 'whose seed does not disappear' does not make the 'that I eat' vow strict in general. It only says the leniency doesn't work when the original forbidden seed is still physically there.
steps.whatToRemember: 'Upon me' forbids the object, so replacements and growths are forbidden. 'That I eat' forbids only the act, so replacements and growths are permitted, unless the seed never disappears.

phrases.english: "...that I eat," or "...that I taste" —
he is permitted in their replacements and in their growths,
with an item whose seed disappears.
But with an item whose seed does not disappear —
even growths of growths are forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts a different wording with step 1 and limits the leniency.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow on the act of eating does not forbid replacements or growths, except for items whose seed remains intact.

steps.title: The same rules apply to a vow on a wife's handiwork
steps.stepSummary: A husband who forbids his wife's handiwork to himself follows the same pattern. 'Upon me' forbids replacements and growths. 'That I eat' permits them, except where the seed does not disappear.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says to his wife 'Your handiwork is קונם upon me,' or 'They are קונם upon my mouth,' or 'They are קונם to my mouth,' he is forbidden in their replacements and growths. If he said '...that I eat' or '...that I taste,' he is permitted in their replacements and growths, with an item whose seed disappears. But with an item whose seed does not disappear, even growths of growths are forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה repeats the exact same two-part rule, now for a husband's vow about the things his wife makes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that the rule depends on the wording, not on what kind of item is involved. Her handiwork is treated just like the fruit: a vow on the object spreads to replacements and growths, and a vow on his eating does not. This sets up the next cases, which are also about her handiwork.

keyTerms.meaning: One who says to his wife
Your handiwork; what you make with your hands

phrases.english: One who says to his wife:
"Your handiwork is konam upon me,"
"They are konam upon my mouth,"
"They are konam to my mouth" —
he is forbidden in their replacements and in their growths.
"...that I eat," "...that I taste" —
he is permitted in their replacements and in their growths,
with an item whose seed disappears.
But an item whose seed does not disappear —
even growths of growths are forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: האומר לאשתו קונם מעשה ידיך עלי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the rules of steps 1–2 to a wife's handiwork.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A vow on a wife's handiwork follows the same wording-based rules as a vow on produce.

steps.title: 'I will not eat until פסח' limits the ban in time
steps.stepSummary: If 'until פסח' is attached to 'I will not eat' or 'I will not cover myself,' then after פסח he may use what she made, even if she made it before פסח.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said 'What you make, I will not eat until פסח,' or 'What you make, I will not cover myself with until פסח,' and she made it before פסח, he is permitted to eat it and cover himself with it after פסח.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה starts a new topic: how the place of the words 'until פסח' in the sentence changes the vow. This is the first of two contrasting cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here 'until פסח' describes his not eating, so the ban itself ends at פסח. Once פסח passes, everything she made is permitted to him, even items made before פסח.

keyTerms.meaning: I will not cover myself, meaning wear clothing she made

phrases.english: "What you make, I will not eat until Pesach,"
"What you make, I will not cover myself with until Pesach,"
if she made it before Pesach —
he is permitted to eat and to cover himself after Pesach.

steps.triggerLanguage: שאת עושה איני אוכל עד הפסח
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When 'until פסח' modifies the eating, the ban ends at פסח.

steps.title: 'What you make until פסח' forbids those items forever
steps.stepSummary: If 'until פסח' is attached to 'what you make,' then whatever she made before פסח stays forbidden to him even after פסח.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said 'What you make until פסח, I will not eat,' or 'What you make until פסח, I will not cover myself with,' and she made it before פסח, he is forbidden to eat it and cover himself with it after פסח.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the opposite case: the same words in a different order, with the opposite result.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now 'until פסח' describes which items are forbidden, namely those she makes before פסח. His ban on those items has no end date, so they stay forbidden even after פסח.

keyTerms.meaning: To eat and to cover oneself

steps.whatToRemember: Watch where 'until פסח' sits. Next to 'I will not eat,' it sets when the ban ends. Next to 'what you make,' it sets which items are banned, and those stay banned for good.

phrases.english: "What you make until Pesach, I will not eat,"

phrases.aramaic: וְ״שֶׁאַתְּ עוֹשָׂה עַד הַפֶּסַח אֵינִי מִתְכַּסֶּה״,
phrases.english: or "What you make until Pesach, I will not cover myself with,"
if she made it before Pesach —
he is forbidden to eat and to cover himself after Pesach.

steps.triggerLanguage: שאת עושה עד הפסח איני אוכל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Mirror image of step 4: same words reordered, opposite ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When 'until פסח' modifies 'what you make,' items made before פסח remain forbidden after פסח.

steps.title: A conditional ban on benefit tied to going to her father's house
steps.stepSummary: A husband forbids his wife to benefit from him until פסח if she goes to her father's house before the festival. If she went before פסח, she is forbidden to benefit from him until פסח.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he said 'Benefit from me is forbidden to you until פסח, if you go to your father's house until the festival,' and she went before פסח, she is forbidden to benefit from him until פסח.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה closes with a conditional vow. There are two time frames here: one for the ban and one for the condition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ban on benefit lasts until פסח, but the condition (her going to her father's house) can happen any time until the festival. If she went before פסח, the condition is met while the ban period is still running, so she is forbidden to benefit from him until פסח.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two time frames. 'Until פסח' is how long the ban lasts. 'Until the festival' is the window in which her going to her father's house counts.

phrases.english: "[Konam] that you benefit from me until Pesach

phrases.aramaic: אִם הוֹלֶכֶת אַתְּ לְבֵית אָבִיךְ עַד הֶחָג״,
phrases.english: if you go to your father's house until the festival,"
if she went before Pesach —
she is forbidden to benefit from him until Pesach.

steps.triggerLanguage: שאת נהנית לי עד הפסח אם הולכת את לבית אביך עד החג
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of time limits in vows, now with a condition attached.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If she fulfills the condition before פסח, the ban on benefit takes effect until פסח.
